summary: Describes NPTv6, a stateless way to swap one IPv6 network prefix for another as packets cross a boundary. Each inside address maps one-to-one to an outside address, giving some of the address independence of IPv4 NAT while keeping end-to-end reachability at the network layer. It is an Experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: When mail leaves a building, the street part of the address is changed but the apartment number stays the same. This does that for IPv6 addresses, so a network can change its outside prefix without renumbering everything inside.

subtitle: Stateless prefix translation for IPv6 networks, checksum-neutral and one-to-one.

tldr.problem: IPv6 networks want address independence—the ability to change upstream providers without renumbering internal systems—but IPv6 discourages provider-independent prefixes, forcing enterprises to either request special status or accept ISP dependency.
tldr.mechanism: NPTv6 stateless translates between an internal prefix (often a ULA) and an external provider-allocated prefix, using a checksum-neutral algorithm that preserves the lower bits, requiring no port mapping or per-flow state, and allowing asymmetric routing and failover.
tldr.outcome: Deployed in some edge networks, NPTv6 enables multihoming and prefix changes without internal renumbering, but at the cost of breaking applications that embed addresses or rely on end-to-end authentication.

today: RFC 6296 is Experimental and has not been widely deployed in production networks. The IETF generally discourages NAT64 (IPv4-to-IPv6 translation) in favor of native IPv6 or dual-stack deployment. Where NPTv6 has been tried, it faces the fundamental challenges of any address translation: application incompatibility and operational complexity. Unique Local Addresses (RFC 4193) with proper renumbering procedures or multihoming with provider-independent addressing are typically preferred.

sections.title: Introduction and Address Independence
sections.content:
Address independence in IPv6 means internal systems keep the same addresses even when the external provider-allocated prefix changes due to ISP switching or multihoming. Unlike IPv4 NAT, NPTv6 is stateless and algorithmic—no per-connection state is maintained, making it compatible with failover, load sharing, and new transport protocols. The trade-off is that NPTv6 cannot offer security through address obscuring (unlike NAPT44), is not compatible with IPsec Authentication Header, and may break applications that transmit IP addresses in their payload (requiring Application Layer Gateways).

The RFC emphasizes that while NPTv6 provides address independence comparable to provider-independent addressing, it requires fewer RIR resources and BGP coordination than PI addressing alternatives.
sections.plainLanguage: NPTv6 lets a network keep its own address space inside, while appearing different to the outside world. When the ISP changes, only the outside changes; inside stays the same.

sections.title: NPTv6 Architecture and Deployment
sections.content:
An NPTv6 Translator sits at the boundary between an internal network (typically using Unique Local Addresses or ULAs from RFC 4193) and an external network with a provider-allocated global prefix. Datagrams are translated algorithmically: outbound traffic has the internal prefix overwritten with the external prefix, and inbound traffic has the destination prefix changed from external to internal.

NPTv6 supports multiple deployment patterns: simple translation (one internal, one external prefix), peer translation (between two private networks), redundancy (multiple translators with the same configuration for load sharing), and multihoming (one internal prefix mapped to multiple external prefixes from different ISPs).
sections.plainLanguage: The translator is on the network border. When traffic leaves, it rewrites the 'from' address. When traffic arrives, it rewrites the 'to' address so packets reach the right inside computer.

sections.title: Checksum-Neutral Translation
sections.content:
NPTv6's key innovation is checksum-neutral mapping: modifying an IP address affects the pseudo-header checksum used by TCP and UDP, but NPTv6 adjusts a different 16-bit word in the address by a complementary amount, so the overall checksum remains unchanged. This avoids the need to recalculate transport-layer checksums.

For /48 or shorter prefixes, the adjustment is applied to the subnet field (bits 48–63), leaving the Interface Identifier untouched. For longer prefixes (/49+), the adjustment is applied to the first available 16-bit word in the IID that is not 0xFFFF, to avoid breaking future protocols that may use unique IIDs. This algorithm works in both directions: the same mapping reverses automatically.

A side effect: networks using a /48 external prefix cannot use subnet 0xFFFF.
sections.plainLanguage: When you change the address, you make a matching opposite change elsewhere in the address so the checksum number (which TCP and UDP use to verify the data wasn't corrupted) stays the same.

sections.title: Behavioral Requirements and Applications
sections.content:
NPTv6 Translators MUST implement hairpinning: when an internal host uses the external address of another internal host, the translator recognizes this, translates both the outbound and inbound legs, and allows the session to proceed. This enables internal nodes to reach each other using external addresses when necessary.

Unlike NAPT44, NPTv6 has few behavioral requirements beyond hairpinning, because it performs no port mapping and maintains no state. However, applications face challenges: an application sees a different address for itself on the inside than on the outside, application referrals break when they embed addresses, and DNS hacks to solve this are incomplete. Split DNS (serving different records inside and outside) and application-layer gateways may be needed for some protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: If one inside computer tries to reach another using the outside address, the translator notice and flips the address back to inside. But programs that mention IP addresses to each other often break.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Cautions
sections.content:
NPTv6 is stateless and permissive, allowing direct inbound connections to internal nodes—the opposite of NAPT44's implicit filtering. While this preserves end-to-end reachability, it removes NAT's incidental security benefits. Administrators MUST deploy a separate firewall to restrict inbound traffic and should implement the simple security capabilities defined in RFC 6092.

NPTv6 is also incompatible with IPsec Authentication Header (which signs the IP header) and incompatible with protocols that authenticate addresses (such as TCP Authentication Option), since the addresses change in transit.

The RFC recommends careful consideration of alternatives (ULAs with global addresses, multihoming with multiple ISPs and routing, Unique Local Addresses with proper renumbering procedures) before deploying NPTv6 in production networks.
sections.plainLanguage: NPTv6 lets anything from the outside reach the inside, so you need a firewall too. And it breaks encryption that protects the IP header itself.
